extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether claim additional elements amount to 'significantly more' than a judicial exception under Step 2B of the §101 subject-matter-eligibility framework. Focuses on whether additional elements are well‑understood, routine, conventional, or otherwise meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well‑understood, routine, conventional activity
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining whether additional elements amount to significantly more than a judicial exception, the examiner should evaluate whether the elements define only well‑understood, routine, conventional activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This consideration overlaps with other Step 2B considerations (improvement, mere instructions to apply an exception, insignificant extra‑solution activity). Key points: (1) Being known in the art does not automatically make an element conventional for eligibility purposes (novelty/obviousness is distinct from eligibility) — see Enfish example; (2) A factual determination is required (Berkheimer) but a prior art search is not always necessary — examiners may rely on what courts or those in the art recognize, including specification statements; (3) Even if individual elements are conventional, their combination can be an inventive concept (Diamond v. Diehr; BASCOM; Rapid Litigation Management). A rejection should be made only if an examiner, relying on expertise, can conclude the additional elements do not amount to significantly more (Step 2B: NO). If elements are beyond those recognized as conventional, they will in most cases amount to significantly more (Step 2B: YES). See MPEP §2106.05 and §2106.07(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Required factual support for conventionality conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: A factual determination that additional element(s) are well‑understood, routine, conventional activity must be expressly supported in writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate forms of support include: (a) citation to an express statement in the specification or applicant prosecution statement indicating the element(s) are well‑understood or conventional; (b) citation to court decisions noting the conventional nature of the element(s); (c) citation to publications demonstrating conventionality; and (d) an explicit statement that the examiner is taking official notice of conventionality. See MPEP §2106.07(a) for more on record support. The analysis parallels the 35 U.S.C. 112(a) standard about what is so well known it need not be described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer functions recognized as well‑understood, routine, conventional
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have recognized certain computer functions as well‑understood, routine, and conventional when claimed at a high level of generality or as insignificant extra‑solution activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representative examples (with case citations): (i) receiving or transmitting data over a network (Symantec; TLI Communications; OIP Techs; buySAFE), (ii) performing repetitive calculations (Flook; Bancorp Services), (iii) electronic recordkeeping (Alice; Ultramercial), (iv) storing and retrieving information in memory (Versata; OIP Techs), (v) scanning/extracting data from documents (Content Extraction; OCR), and (vi) web browser back/forward functionality (Internet Patent Corp.). Note the listing is not exhaustive and does not imply that all computer functions or any generic computer implementation are necessarily conventional or ineligible — see DDR Holdings, Amdocs, BASCOM for distinctions where generic components in combination provided a technical improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laboratory techniques recognized as well‑understood, routine, conventional
rubrics_metrics.description: In the life sciences, certain laboratory techniques have been recognized by courts as well‑understood, routine, and conventional when recited generically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representative examples (with case citations): determining a biomarker level in blood (Mayo; Cleveland Clinic), using PCR to amplify/detect DNA (Genetic Techs; Ariosa/Sequenom), detecting DNA/enzymes in a sample (Sequenom; Cleveland Clinic), immunizing a patient (Classen), analyzing DNA for sequence or allelic variants (Genetic Techs), freezing and thawing cells (Rapid Litigation Mgmt.), amplifying/sequencing nucleic acids (University of Utah v. Ambry), and hybridizing a gene probe (Ambry). When claimed merely at a high level, these techniques may be conventional or insignificant extra‑solution activity for eligibility purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other activities courts have found well‑understood or conventional
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have identified additional nontechnical activities as well‑understood, routine, or conventional when claimed in a merely generic manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representative examples (with case citations): recording a customer's order (Apple v. Ameranth), shuffling/dealing a standard deck of cards (In re Smith), restricting public access by requiring viewing an advertisement (Ultramercial), presenting offers and gathering statistics (OIP Techs), determining an estimated outcome and setting a price (OIP Techs), and arranging/sorting information and determining price (Versata). These may be conventional or mere extra‑solution activity depending on claim specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other meaningful limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim should add meaningful limitations beyond generally linking use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment to transform the judicial exception into patent‑eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The phrase 'meaningful limitations' describes additional elements that provide an inventive concept or integrate the judicial exception into a practical application. Considerations in MPEP §2106.05(a)-(d) may constitute meaningful limitations when they amount to significantly more or integrate the exception. Examples: Diamond v. Diehr (Arrhenius equation integrated into rubber‑molding process — meaningful limitations), contrasted with Alice (data processing system and communications controllers merely linked the abstract idea to computers). Classen is an example where an immunization step integrated analytical results into a tangible treatment. Examine additional elements both individually and in combination; combinations can render the claim eligible even if individual elements do not. Examiners may explain on the record why additional elements meaningfully limit the exception. Note overlap with treatment/prophylaxis considerations in Step 2A Prong Two (MPEP §2106.04(d)(2)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere instructions to apply an exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether additional elements amount to more than reciting 'apply it' — i.e., whether the claim does more than merely instruct implementing a judicial exception on a generic computer or by generic steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court guidance: additional elements must do 'more than simply state the [judicial exception] while adding the words ‘apply it’' (Alice quoting Mayo). Examples where courts found mere instructions: Mayo (measuring metabolites in any known way), Alice (intermediated settlement implemented by a generic computer), Benson (BCD‑to‑binary process with no meaningful practical application except with a computer). Claims that amount to nothing more than instructions to apply an abstract idea using a generic computer are not eligible. Requiring more than mere instructions does not require claim narrowness — courts have found both broad claims eligible (McRO; Thales) and narrow claims ineligible (Ultramercial; Electric Power Group).
